claims.text: Isoniazid 5 mg/kg (usually max 300 mg) PO daily.
claims.quote: Isoniazid (INH) dosage is usually 5 mg/kg (typically a maximum of 300 mg) orally once/day for adults

claims.text: ADRs: rash, fever, hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, rarely anemia/agranulocytosis; safe in pregnancy.
claims.quote: Potential adverse effects of INH include rash, fever, hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, and, rarely, anemia and agranulocytosis. INH is safe during pregnancy.

claims.text: Hepatitis risk higher if >35 y, alcohol use disorder, chronic liver disease, postpartum.
claims.quote: Clinical hepatitis occurs more often in patients with the following characteristics: > 35 years old, alcohol use disorder, chronic liver disease, and postpartum.

claims.text: Serial LFTs only if liver-disease risk factors.
claims.quote: Monitoring with serial liver tests is not recommended unless patients have risk factors for liver disease.

claims.text: If fatigue, anorexia, nausea, vomiting or jaundice: stop and check LFTs.
claims.quote: Symptoms of hepatotoxicity include unexplained fatigue, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, or jaundice. If these symptoms occur, treatment is suspended, and liver tests are done.
Pyridoxine 25 to 50 mg orally once/day can prevent this complication

claims.text: in at-risk patients (pregnant/breastfeeding, malnourished, DM, HIV, alcohol use, older).
claims.quote: Peripheral neuropathy can result from INH-induced pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiency, most likely in patients with the following characteristics: pregnant or breastfeeding, undernutrition, diabetes mellitus, HIV infection, alcohol use disorder, cancer, uremia, and older adult.

claims.text: INH slows phenytoin metabolism (lower phenytoin dose); significant reaction with disulfiram.
claims.quote: INH delays hepatic metabolism of phenytoin, requiring dose reduction. It can also cause a significant reaction to disulfiram
